title: Surgical Antibiotic Prophylaxis
sources: Critical Vector — Anesthesia Reference: Surgical Antibiotic Prophylaxis (ASHP/IDSA/SHEA 2023)
ASHP/IDSA/SHEA/SIS Clinical Practice Guidelines for Antimicrobial Prophylaxis in Surgery

changelog.change: Initial entry — general principles, agent dosing + redose intervals table, and procedure-specific selection with penicillin-allergy alternatives.

summary: Give within 60 minutes of incision (120 minutes for vancomycin or a fluoroquinolone). Redose intraoperatively at 1–2× the drug's half-life, or after > 1500 mL blood loss. Stop within 24 hours postoperatively (48 hours for cardiac surgery). A single dose is adequate for most procedures.

items: Administer within 60 min of incision — 120 min for vancomycin and fluoroquinolones (longer infusion).
Redose at 1–2× the drug half-life from the first dose, or if estimated blood loss > 1500 mL.
Discontinue within 24 h postoperatively (cardiac surgery: 48 h). Continuing longer does not reduce SSI and drives resistance and C. difficile.
Weight-adjust: cefazolin 2 g standard, 3 g if ≥ 120 kg.

rows: 15–20 mg/kg IV (max 3 g); AUC/MIC-guided, target AUC 400–600 mg·h/L

body.text: For Caesarean section, give the prophylactic dose BEFORE incision (not after cord clamp) — this halves endometritis and wound infection without harming the neonate. Redose cefazolin q4h if the operation is prolonged or blood loss exceeds 1500 mL.

A reported penicillin allergy is often not a true one — a history of a non-severe reaction (rash without anaphylaxis, > 10 years ago) does not contraindicate cefazolin, which shares no relevant side chain with penicillins. Reserve vancomycin/clindamycin for genuine severe reactions, as they are less effective for SSI prevention.
